We are about to explore this across several turns. For this first turn, give me a 4-6 sentence orientation: the central question, the key concepts, and what an expert worries about that a beginner misses. Be concrete and avoid platitudes.

At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write the single sharpest follow-up question a teacher would ask next. Do not mention or quote the trace token. (trace-10)
response:
Softmax outputs produce a probability distribution over classes, and the central question of calibration is whether those numbers mean what they claim: if a model outputs 0.9 for class A across many inputs, does class A actually occur 90% of the time? The key concepts are reliability diagrams (binning predictions by confidence and plotting mean confidence vs. actual accuracy per bin), Expected Calibration Error (ECE) (the weighted average of |confidence − accuracy| across bins), and the distinction between sharpness (how peaked the distribution is) and calibration (whether the peaks are honest). A model can be simultaneously overconfident and accurate — high accuracy masks poor calibration — which trips up beginners who conflate the two. What experts worry about that beginners miss: ECE is acutely sensitive to the number and placement of bins, and because predictions cluster near 0 and 1 in modern networks (a consequence of depth and ReLU stacking), coarse equal-width binning produces nearly empty middle bins that contribute noise rather than signal. The deeper concern is that post-hoc fixes like temperature scaling can make ECE look good while leaving conditional calibration broken — the model may be well-calibrated on average but badly miscalibrated on specific subgroups or input regions that matter clinically or legally.

NEXT: Why does temperature scaling improve ECE so reliably on held-out data, and what structural property of softmax outputs makes it almost too easy a fix?

Softmax outputs in neural classifiers are systematically overconfident: a model outputting 0.95 for a class is often correct far less than 95% of the time, a phenomenon quantified in the landmark 2017 paper On Calibration of Modern Neural Networks (Guo et al.), which showed that ResNet-110 on CIFAR-100 had an Expected Calibration Error (ECE) of ~17% before temperature scaling, dropping to ~3% after. ECE is computed by bucketing predictions into M equal-width confidence bins (typically 15), computing the absolute gap between mean confidence and empirical accuracy within each bin, then taking a sample-weighted average across bins — a deceptively simple metric that hides a critical flaw: because bins are fixed-width, low-confidence regions (where most predictions cluster) dominate the estimate, masking poor calibration in the high-confidence tail. This pathology motivated Adaptive Calibration Error (ACE) and classwise-ECE, introduced by Nixon et al. (2019), which use equal-mass bins or per-class decomposition to surface miscalibration that standard ECE overlooks. Temperature scaling — dividing the logit vector by a scalar T learned on a validation set — remains the gold standard fix for global calibration, but it leaves classwise calibration largely intact or even worsens it, because a single scalar cannot simultaneously correct the heterogeneous overconfidence profiles of individual classes in large-vocabulary models like ImageNet classifiers. A subtler issue: ECE is not a proper scoring rule (unlike log-loss or Brier score), so optimizing ECE directly can paradoxically produce worse probabilistic predictions while appearing well-calibrated in the bins.

Temperature scaling finds a scalar T > 1 that softens overconfident in-distribution (ID) logits, but out-of-distribution (OOD) inputs typically produce lower-norm logit vectors to begin with — the model is already less peaked — so applying the same T over-flattens OOD softmax outputs, pushing confidence toward the uniform distribution and making the model appear more uncertain than its actual (already poor) discriminative signal warrants, which Ovadia et al. (2019, "Can You Trust Your Model's Uncertainty?") demonstrated empirically across dataset-shift benchmarks where temperature-scaled deterministic networks degraded in calibration faster under shift than even vanilla models in some regimes. The geometric root cause is that ID and OOD inputs occupy different regions of logit-norm space: ID inputs cluster at high logit norms (sharp simplex vertices), while OOD inputs cluster near the origin, and a single global temperature is equivalent to a radial rescaling that cannot simultaneously correct both clusters — it is, in effect, fitting a one-parameter family of hyperspherical rescalings to a bimodal distribution of norms. This was made precise by Ming et al. and related work showing that logit norm is itself a strong OOD detector, implying that norm and direction carry independent calibration-relevant information that scalar temperature discards. Desai & Durrett (2020) further showed on NLP classifiers that temperature scaling trained on ID validation sets can increase ECE by 2–5 percentage points on domain-shifted test sets, precisely because the chosen T assumes the ID logit-norm distribution. The fix attempted by methods like vector scaling or Dirichlet calibration is to apply a full diagonal (or dense) linear transform to the logit vector before softmax, allowing independent rescaling per class and partial decoupling of norm from direction — though these still generalize poorly under large covariate shift because the transform is fit on ID data.

Logit norm (the L2 norm of the pre-softmax logits) correlates with OOD-ness because in-distribution inputs tend to produce high-magnitude logit vectors, but using it as a raw confidence threshold breaks down under feature collapse and training distribution shift: models trained with cross-entropy aggressively push in-distribution logit norms up, so near-OOD inputs that share surface features with training data (e.g., CIFAR-10 vs. CIFAR-100) still produce inflated norms — Ming et al. (2023, "How to Exploit Hyperspherical Uniformity") showed AUROC on near-OOD benchmarks drops to near-chance for norm-based detectors when semantic overlap is high. Separately, logit norm and softmax confidence are not independent: dividing by the norm (i.e., using the cosine logit) removes magnitude information entirely, so you recover calibration near class boundaries but destroy the OOD signal — this is the core tension in the NormFace / CosFace family. A theoretically grounded joint treatment comes from energy-based models: Grathwohl et al.'s JEM (2020) reinterprets the classifier's free energy — log-sum-exp of logits — as an unnormalized data density, so the same scalar simultaneously drives confidence calibration (via temperature scaling on energy) and OOD detection (in-distribution data has lower free energy), with AUROC improvements of ~10 points over MSP on CIFAR-100 vs. SVHN. The practical failure mode of JEM is training instability and cost (SGLD sampling), but DICE (Sun & Li, 2022) and VIM (Wang et al., 2022) offer lighter alternatives that sparsify or decompose the weight matrix to align the confidence and OOD objectives geometrically, without generative training. The deepest theoretical issue is that calibration is a marginal property (correctness conditional on confidence level) while OOD detection is a support property (is this point in the training manifold?), and these only coincide when the model's learned representation is perfectly class-conditional Gaussian — which Deep Deterministic Uncertainty (DDU, Mukhoti et al., 2023) explicitly enforces via spectral normalization to make the feature-space density a valid proxy for both.

A non-obvious implication is that ECE is not proper in the formal sense — it can be gamed by a model that abstains on uncertain inputs or deliberately misclusters confidence to minimize bin averages without improving actual reliability, which is why proper scoring rules like the Brier score or log-loss are often preferable for optimization even when ECE is used for reporting.

Calibration and representation quality are not fundamentally in tension, but they are optimized by different geometric properties of the same layer, and the conflict originates specifically at the penultimate (pre-logit) layer where the linear classifier head reads off features: good discrimination requires tight, well-separated clusters (high within-class concentration, large between-class margin), while naive calibration — as enforced by cross-entropy with uniform smoothing — penalizes overconfident outputs by pulling cluster means toward the origin and reducing norm variance, which degrades the linear separability that makes representations transferable. Kornblith et al. and subsequent work on neural collapse (Papyan et al., 2020) showed that in the terminal phase of training, the penultimate features of a perfectly trained classifier converge to a simplex equiangular tight frame (ETF) — maximally spread, equal-norm vertices — and this ETF geometry simultaneously maximizes linear discriminability and produces well-calibrated softmax outputs, suggesting the tension is an artifact of incomplete training or regularization that perturbs the ETF, not an intrinsic property of the geometry. Label smoothing specifically disrupts ETF convergence by biasing the cross-entropy gradient to resist the final collapse of within-class variance, keeping cluster means slightly off their ETF vertices — Zhu et al. (2021) measured that label smoothing with ε=0.1 reduced the NC1 metric (within-class variability relative to between-class variability) by ~30% compared to hard-label training on CIFAR-100, confirming the geometric distortion. The practical resolution is post-hoc calibration on top of hard-label-trained ETF-geometry models: train with hard labels to convergence (achieving tight ETF structure and good representations), then apply temperature scaling or Platt scaling, which corrects the overconfidence without disturbing the penultimate geometry since it operates only on the logit layer. This is why the Guo et al. (2017) finding that older, smaller networks were better calibrated than ResNets makes sense in hindsight — shallower networks with less capacity never fully committed to the high-norm, low-entropy ETF geometry, so they appeared calibrated by accident, but at the cost of weaker representations.

Answer in 4-7 sentences. Be concrete; cite specific systems, papers, or numbers where useful. At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write your single sharpest non-obvious follow-up question, different from any we have asked before. Do not mention the trace token. (trace-17)
response:
CLIP's miscalibration is severe and well-documented — Minderer et al. (2021, "Revisiting the Calibration of Modern Neural Networks") showed that zero-shot CLIP on ImageNet had ECE of ~15–20% depending on prompt, far worse than a comparably accurate supervised ResNet — and the non-ETF classifier geometry is a major but incomplete explanation. The core geometric problem is that CLIP's classifier weights are text embeddings of class names, which live in a language-shaped subspace of the joint embedding space: these vectors are not orthogonal, not equal-norm, and not arranged as an ETF — semantically similar classes (e.g., "cat" and "kitten") have cosine similarities of 0.7–0.9, meaning the linear classifier has nearly collinear columns, which produces systematically inflated softmax probabilities for semantically proximate classes and deflated ones for isolated classes, directly manufacturing miscalibration that has nothing to do with the image encoder's feature geometry. However, the non-ETF geometry doesn't fully explain it: a second independent cause is the contrastive training objective itself, which optimizes image-text alignment across a batch of N pairs with an InfoNCE loss effectively using temperature 1/τ (τ≈0.07 in original CLIP), producing logit scales ~14× larger than supervised cross-entropy training — this means the raw cosine similarities, when converted to logits, are already in a regime where softmax is extremely peaked, so the model is structurally overconfident before any class-name geometry is considered. Parashar et al. and subsequent prompt-engineering work showed that even with perfect ETF-arranged prompt embeddings (constructed synthetically), CLIP's ECE only improved to ~8–10%, confirming that the logit-scale problem from contrastive training contributes roughly half the miscalibration independently of classifier geometry. The practically important corollary is that temperature scaling is unusually effective for CLIP — because the dominant miscalibration source is a global logit-scale inflation from τ, a single scalar T can undo most of it, and indeed Minderer et al. found temperature scaling reduced CLIP's ECE from ~17% to ~3–4%, a larger absolute improvement than for any supervised model class they tested.
